children: New Delhi, Nov. 16 -- To sustain the momentum of Aatmanirbharta (self-reliance) and build enduring military capabilities, India's private defence sector needs faster decision-making, predictable order pipelines, and expedited testing, backed by the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to eliminate bureaucratic procurement bottlenecks, top industry leaders said on Monday.

Speaking at the ANI National Security Summit 3.0 in New Delhi, Raphe mPhibr Chairman Vikas Mishra and Nibe Limited Executive Director Balaji Sominathan called for structural reforms across procurement rules, banking cycles, and vendor evaluation criteria so domestic firms can scale up and own core defence technologies.

Highlighting how overworked procurement officials struggle with massive paperwork, Vikas Mishra pitched deploying AI to draft complex tender documents-such as Requests for Information (RFI), Requests for Proposal (RFP), and Expressions of Interest (EoI)-which he estimated could double or triple acquisition speeds.

"One thing which we really need is faster decision-making, which a lot of governments outside are taking help of AI for. For example, the generation of an RFI or RFP-in a process which could be 10 pages or 1,000 pages because of the complexity of the system-takes a lot of time," Mishra said. "In the forces, one person is going there on Saturdays and Sundays handling 40 projects. There is a lot of work in developing that, so we know why the delays are happening. They are not intentional delays."

Noting that drafting an RFP even for a standard military truck runs into nearly 120 pages as a binding legal contract, he added: "Bringing AI into these things is one of the easiest ways to introduce AI into defence and see how it affects our system. If you can just speed up the process of RFI, RFP, and EoI making, things will get twice or thrice faster."

Mishra also urged policymakers to replace static regulations with greater policy dynamism and institutional backing for officials willing to take calculated risks. "As we are growing, we are moving towards it, but we are not there yet. Static policies remain; we don't have dynamism in policy," he said. "Then there is the ability to take risks-because if you make a decision that you know is good for the country, but it involves taking a risk under the General Financial Rules (GFR), why would you take that risk if you could end up in jail? Defence is a tricky business in that way."
Beyond the Ministry of Defence (MoD), Mishra flagged that traditional 90-day banking norms clash sharply with the realities of defence manufacturing and rigorous military trials.

"Any product which we make takes a minimum of 12 months up to delivery. Suppose you have taken a loan from a bank-when delivery doesn't happen immediately because it takes time in testing, the bank says you have defaulted," Mishra explained. "As a country, we need to make this shift as a whole. The Ministry of Finance also needs to understand that banks need to give a little more leverage and look at the defence vertical differently, because this cycle cannot be a 90-day cycle."

Nibe Limited Executive Director Balaji Sominathan emphasised that while the government has taken substantial foundational steps, policy must now evolve from merely inviting private players to actively enabling them across three critical pillars -- order predictability, speedy testing & validation and clear operational requirements.

"From having a policy where you are encouraging private participation, we need to work more towards how we can enable the Indian private sector. We need predictability. The private sector is making investments, but without predictability, it is going to be difficult for us to sustain in the long run. On the testing front, there has to be a speedy validation and testing process for products when we go to government entities. A proper operational requirement has to be articulated to the industry. That is very important," said Sominathan.

Sominathan also urged a rethink of tender eligibility norms that judge deep-tech firms solely on past balance sheets rather than future engineering capability. "This is basically a technology-driven sector. Right now, Indian private firms are evaluated based on our balance sheets and turnover. You can't evaluate companies that can build great technologies tomorrow based on their current balance sheet. We need brainstorming to work out a solution for that," he said.
Both leaders forcefully rejected perceptions that Indian private firms merely assemble foreign kits, pointing to massive domestic infrastructure and indigenous intellectual property.

Mishra noted that Raphe mPhibr's 700,000-square-foot facility is the largest of its kind in India and among the six largest globally-so advanced that foreign observers documented its manufacturing processes for their own engineers.

Detailing his company's portfolio of offensive and protective systems, Mishra revealed: "These drones range from platforms that can lift 5 kilograms up to 600 kilograms-a thousand times bigger than standard camera drones-including a 15-metre wingspan Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) class UAV that we are about to supply, alongside multicopters and fixed-wing drones. We make our own engines, our own electronics, our own structures-everything."

Sharing an eye-opening example from Nibe's universal rocket launcher programme, Sominathan noted that while the firm has a technology collaboration with an Israeli Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM), an audit revealed that 70 to 80 per cent of the supply chain already resides in India.

"The Israelis were actually manufacturing the rocket components here. All the components went to Israel, where they integrated them and sent them back to us at a marked-up price. Now, private sectors are putting efforts into reducing remaining technology dependencies to move toward complete technology ownership."

Sominathan highlighted Nibe's sprawling 200-acre manufacturing hub in Shirdi-housing 11 facilities of 2 lakh square feet each-capable of producing 5 lakh bombs annually alongside rocket launcher systems to sustain the armed forces during wartime.

"When you build with a foreign design, you are building a product. When you build with your own design, you are building capability. At Nibe, we are investing in building globally competitive capabilities for both exports and our armed forces," he said.

Addressing historical mistrust toward private defence players, Sominathan said the ecosystem has undergone a decisive transformation from the days when state-owned enterprises alone supplied the military.

"It is not PSUs versus the private sector; it is PSUs plus the private sector, plus startups, plus academia," Sominathan said. "PSUs bring large institutional infrastructure and manufacturing depth; private companies bring agility, speed, and risk-taking ability; startups bring disruptive thinking; and academia brings fundamental research. The real opportunity lies in bringing all these capabilities together."

As India marks its 80th Independence Day, this deepening synergy between public institutions, private innovators, and academia underscores a decade-long transformation-cementing India's emergence as a stronger, self-reliant, and globally credible defence power capable of safeguarding its sovereignty and contributing to global security.

title: 'Deploy AI to cut procurement delays, move from encouraging to enabling': Pvt defence leaders call for faster testing, predictable orders
